summary: Describes how to use information attached to a trust anchor public key when validating certification paths. The information can constrain the trust anchor, typically limiting the policies and names allowed in validated paths. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A trusted person might be trusted for only some things. This explains how to follow those limits when checking a chain of certificates.

questions: certification path validation with trust anchors
how are trust anchor constraints enforced
what constraints can limit a root certificate
subtitle: How to enforce limits on what a trusted certificate signer can certify

tldr.problem: When a public key is trusted as a certification authority, it may need to be limited to certifying only certain types of certificates or names. The RFC 5280 base standard allows constraints but does not specify how to enforce them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines initialization rules for the RFC 5280 path validation algorithm that extract constraints from the trust anchor and apply them to the validation process, limiting permitted names, certificate policies, and path length.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now enforce trust anchor constraints consistently, preventing scenarios where a trusted key accidentally validates certificates outside its intended scope.

today: RFC 5937 is an Informational RFC that defines how to enforce trust anchor constraints in X.509 certification path validation. It has not been obsoleted and remains the standard reference for this mechanism.

sections.title: Introduction to Trust Anchor Constraints
sections.content:
Trust anchors are the root certificates that applications use to verify certification paths. RFC 5280 defines how to validate a chain of certificates but permits (but does not require) implementations to enforce constraints attached to a trust anchor. This document specifies exactly how to do that enforcement.

A trust anchor constraint limits what certificates the trust anchor can issue or endorse. For example, a trust anchor might be allowed to certify only certain names or only certificates under specific policies. Without consistent rules, different applications may enforce constraints differently, creating security risks or interoperability problems.
sections.plainLanguage: A trusted person can be trusted for some things but not others. This explains the clear rules for what a trusted signer is allowed to do.

sections.title: Identifying Trust Anchor Constraints
sections.content:
The Trust Anchor Format (RFC 5914) can represent trust anchors in three ways: as a TrustAnchorInfo structure, as a complete certificate, or as just the certificate data (TBSCertificate). All three can carry constraints using standard X.509 certificate extensions.

Constraints appear as extensions like certificate policies, policy constraints, name constraints, and basic constraints. In the TrustAnchorInfo structure, some constraints (such as certificate policies and name constraints) appear in a special CertPathControls field instead of as extensions. When processing a trust anchor, implementations MUST enforce any constraints marked critical and MAY accept those marked non-critical if recognized.
sections.plainLanguage: The limits are stored in special data fields attached to the trusted signer. Some limits are marked as very important and must never be ignored.

sections.title: Using Constraints During Path Validation
sections.content:
RFC 5280 defines a path validation algorithm with inputs like initial permitted names, certificate policies, and other values. This RFC specifies how to initialize those inputs from the trust anchor's constraints.

If a trust anchor has name constraints, the permitted and excluded name ranges from the anchor are intersected or unioned with any user-provided ranges. If the trust anchor specifies allowed certificate policies, those are intersected with the user-supplied policies. Boolean flags like inhibit-any-policy are activated if present in the trust anchor. A path length constraint from the trust anchor sets the maximum depth of the certified chain.

These initialization steps must occur before the main RFC 5280 validation algorithm runs. After initialization, the standard algorithm proceeds without modification.
sections.plainLanguage: Before checking a chain of certificates, the algorithm starts with the limits from the trusted signer, then applies the normal checking rules.

sections.title: Implementation Approaches
sections.content:
The constraint initialization can be done in two ways. One approach is to integrate it directly into an RFC 5280 implementation, modifying the initialization steps. The other is to implement it as a preprocessing wrapper that adjusts the inputs to an existing RFC 5280 implementation.

For constraints on names and policies, preprocessing is straightforward because RFC 5280 accepts configurable initial values. However, the basic constraints path-length limit cannot be preprocessed since RFC 5280 does not expose a corresponding input parameter. It must instead be validated as post-processing by checking the returned path length.

Some constraint types (such as CMS Content Constraints) may require additional implementation work beyond what this document specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: The limits can be checked before or after the main algorithm, as long as the final result respects all the limits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Applications that do not enforce trust anchor constraints may accept certificates rejected by implementations that do enforce them. For example, an application ignoring a certificate-policy constraint on a trust anchor might accept a certificate under a lower-assurance policy than intended. This is a security weakness that undermines the purpose of the constraints.

Trust anchor information must be securely stored. Modifying a trust anchor to remove constraints could cause the application to accept certificates that should be rejected. Adding unauthorized trust anchors could cause unexpected validation results. The Trust Anchor Format specification (RFC 5914) and the Trust Anchor Management Protocol (RFC 5934) provide additional guidance on secure management of trust anchors.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ignore the limits on a trusted signer, you might accidentally trust something you shouldn't. Keeping the trust information safe is very important.
